name: Cities the World Forgot
description: From Stone Age mounds to a Soviet atomic town: thirty-odd places that were once full of people, and what emptied them.

checkpoints.name: Before the written word
checkpoints.note: The oldest ruins belong to people who left no names. Hilltop pillars, mud-brick towns and the planned streets of the Indus cities were all abandoned, buried or lost, and archaeologists must read them from the ground.

checkpoints.name: Capitals of early empires
checkpoints.note: Ur, Babylon, Nineveh and Troy were famous in their own day. Ur, Babylon and Nineveh lay under desert mounds and Troy under a hill in Anatolia until excavators of the 1800s and 1900s dug them up, and Mesopotamian clay tablets were read again.

checkpoints.name: Classical endings
checkpoints.note: Persepolis burned, Carthage was razed, Ephesus lost its harbour and Pompeii vanished under ash in a single day. In the Americas, Teotihuacan emptied out and Tikal began its long decline, for reasons still debated.

checkpoints.name: Medieval capitals
checkpoints.note: Angkor, Bagan, Cahokia and Great Zimbabwe each ruled a region and each was left behind as trade, climate or enemies shifted. Their stone and earth still stand in the forest and the fields.

checkpoints.name: Gone in a lifetime
checkpoints.note: Conquest ended Tenochtitlan and Machu Picchu, and a missing colony haunts American history. Modern emptiness can be fast: a mining island and a nuclear town were left within weeks or days, while a desert diamond town faded over decades.
